newsitem.title: FRANCE: Suez-Lyonnaise link makes sense - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Suez-Lyonnaise link makes sense - analysts.

text.p: A merger between holding company Cie de Suez and utility group Lyonnaise des Eaux, which the market predicts with growing confidence, would create France's ninth biggest company in market value and give new impetus to both firms, analysts said on Monday.
"Lyonnaise does not have the financial means to realise its ambitions. A link with Suez would give it a big boost," one analyst said on Monday.
"People would like to see it modelled in a way like the Generale (Generale des Eaux)," he added.

Spokeswomen for Suez and Lyonnaise declined comment on Monday on newspaper reports that the two were preparing a merger. But analysts said they were now thinking not whether it would happen but what the terms would be.
Suez ranks 20th in France with a market capitalisation of 45.8 billion francs ($8 billion) and Lyonnaise holds 30th place with a value of 33.2 billion, data from Reuters Securities 3000 shows.
Combined at 79 billion, they would come between the 91.9 billion of Generale des Eaux and the 71.8 billion of glassmaker Compagnie de Saint-Gobain.
Suez, established nearly 140 years ago to finance the building of the Suez canal, has recently been cutting its activities back to purge property-related losses.
The cutbacks, made by Gerard Mestrallet, chairman since July 1995, left the company with "lots of assets but without a clear business", one financial analyst said.
Analysts said the deal would make sense for Suez which has lost its raison d'etre after selling most of its assets including its crown jewel, Banque Indosuez.
Its fate is typical of France's big holding companies, which have gone out of fashion as shareholders insist on getting more value out of their shares.
Groupe Paribas, Suez's traditional rival, is divesting non-strategic assets to refocus on core businesses.
Lyonnaise des Eaux, meanwhile, is still smarting from a 1990 merger with building group Dumez and has also had to carry heavy property losses.
It is active in pure water purification and distribution, as well as in the media, with a stake in French terrestrial television channel M6 and the TPS satellite television venture.
The big attraction for Lyonnaise would not be to create a new giant holding company but Suez's cash hoard.
Lyonnaise, whose main businesses are water contracts, construction and energy, has high hopes for global expansion but lacks the resources to finance growth, the analysts said.
Analyst Jean-Baptiste Bellon at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said he expected Suez to bid for the Lyonnaise shares, either in paper or in cash.
"Debt would perhaps facilitate the operation but it would burden the new group. It's more likely to be in paper," he said.
Based on the company's market values, a paper bid could be two Suez shares for one Lyonnaise.

Suez had shareholders equity of 41.46 billion francs at the end of 1995. It obtained important cash and liquid assets after the sale of investment bank Banque Indosuez and of a four billion franc property loan porfolio to U.S. fund Whitehall.
It also has an unused tax credit estimated at nine billion francs -- allowing the group to avoid paying three billion francs in taxes on future profits.
It made a 1995 net attributable loss of 3.96 billion francs and analysts expect it to report a 1996 net profit of about 1.147 billion francs, doubling to 2.585 billion in 1997.

Lyonnaise has shareholders funds of 16.46 billion, made a 1995 net attributable profit of 906 million francs and is expected by analysts to show a 1996 net profit of 1.26 billion, rising slightly to 1.6 billion in 1997.

Suez has an 16.8 percent stake in Lyonnaise and has 20 percent of voting rights. Insurer Axa-UAP has a 4.4 percent stake in Lyonnaise, Credit Agricole 3.3 percent and Spain's Aguas de Barcelona 1.4 percent.

Suez's main assets are in Belgium, through Societe Generale de Belgique, with a stake in utilities group Tractebel, bank Generale de Banque, financial group Fortis and non-ferrous metals group Union Miniere.

Suez's main shareholders are Credit Agricole with 7.5 percent, Saint-Gobain with 6.2 percent, Banque Nationale de Paris with 5.5 percent, insurer Axa-UAP with 5.46 percent and Belgium's Groupe Bruxelles Lambert with more than six percent.

Suez board members include Saint-Gobain's Jean-Louis Beffa, oil company Elf-Aquitaine head Philippe Jaffre, Credit Agricole's Lucien Douroux, Jacques Friedmann, chairman of the supervisory board of Axa-UAP and Lyonnaise's Monod.
